strengths: The paper addresses an important phenomenon: adversarially trained networks can retain good clean accuracy while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. Connecting representation complexity with training dynamics is a worthwhile objective.

The proposed mechanism—partial learning of shared signal combined with memorization of example-specific noise—is interpretable. The structured model provides explicit quantities for investigating these two behaviors.
Experiments span MNIST, CIFAR10, and synthetic data, with additional neighborhood-flatness diagnostics. These observations provide useful motivation for the proposed explanation.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under the stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on ±2e₁, radius δ=1, and clean classifier f(x)=x₁−1.5. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3. With growing sample size, both atoms occur with substantial empirical frequency, so vanishing robust training error requires correctly classifying both perturbation balls, implying zero robust test error. Thus a CGRO classifier need not exist. The construction needs assumptions controlling how much population mass is covered by training neighborhoods.

The representation proof has additional substantive gaps. Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes, but the proof incorrectly concludes that all training balls are disjoint; overlapping same-class balls invalidate the displayed algebraic rewriting. Appendix F.1 also claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous indicator-based function by continuous ReLU networks. Smoothing does not provide this uniform guarantee, and transferring approximation error to classification error requires additional margin arguments.

Theorem 5.9 conflates different threat models. Training permits perturbations only along the informative patch's signal direction and freezes every noise patch, whereas Definition 3.3 measures robustness over the full norm ball. Small restricted training loss therefore does not establish the claimed robust training error. Indeed, under Assumption 5.7, the combined noise norm is o(α); a full ℓ2 attack can flip and amplify the memorized noise within the radius while preserving the signal. With α^q U and V both of constant order, this can reverse the prediction.

The clean-generalization proof in Appendix E.12 uses an incorrect concentration claim: sums of cubic Gaussian projections are treated as sub-Gaussian. A nondegenerate Gaussian cubic has heavier tails, and projections through different filters are correlated. The asserted residual-weight norm bounds also do not follow from aggregate memorization values. Consequently, the supplied argument does not establish the clean-error guarantee.

The empirical validation does not resolve these theoretical concerns. Section 6.2 sets δ=α=10, contradicting the theorem's strict δ<α condition and allowing complete removal of the informative patch. Only one small synthetic configuration is reported. The real-data capacity sweeps and flatness curves do not distinguish the proposed mechanism from optimization or sample-size effects. Missing attack iterations, step sizes, restarts, and variability across runs further limit reproducibility and assessment of the reported robustness.

The claimed originality of the lower-bound extension needs clarification. Theorem 4.7 is existential over distributions, and a linear clean classifier already satisfies the polynomial-size classifier assumption; broadening that assumption alone does not strengthen the cited linear-separable existence result. Moreover, the worst-case lower bound does not establish a capacity barrier for the structured distribution or experimental datasets. The conceptual combination has merit, but the unsupported principal theorems prevent acceptance.
